To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the obese subjects in this investigation retained sodium in excess of their sodium deficit, and that this sodium retention was associated with a decrease in aldosterone secretion.
the sodium retention that follows a prolonged period of sodium chloride deprivation in obese subjects is markedly and persistently enhanced by a prior period of total fasting.
the obese subjects studied had marked and persistent sodium deficits, which were not completely replenished by sodium intake and re-feeding.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of sodium balance in obese subjects who have been deprived of sodium chloride and food for prolonged periods of time.

the study of the effects of sodium chloride administration in obese patients with and without prior fasting, and the effects of sodium deprivation on sodium balance in obese patients who were previously fasted.
the study of the mechanisms that regulate the renal handling of sodium in man.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the results of these studies indicate that in previously fasted obese subjects with sodium deficits resulting from natriuresis during fasting and continued sodium deprivation, resumption of sodium chloride intake with or without refeeding results in sodium retention that replenishes the previously existing deficits.

the sodium retention observed during the first 5-7 days of sodium refeeding after a period of total fast and sodium deprivation was a consequence of a marked reduction in the renal sodium chloride excretion and not due to a decrease in the glomerular filtration rate or in the renal blood flow, as previously reported by others.
the sodium retention seen in obese subjects who were sodium-deprived during a fast was due to the sodium-deprived fast, not the obesity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

sodium deprivation and refeeding in obese subjects result in marked and persistent sodium and water retention, which is associated with a decrease in sodium chloride space and a decrease in aldosterone secretion rates.

we have shown that the kidney of the obese subject has a remarkable ability to adapt to a variety of stresses, and that the kidney of this subject is capable of handling sodium in a manner that would allow the maintenance of sodium balance under circumstances that would lead to marked sodium retention in the lean subject.
sodium retention is not a consequence of fasting or of sodium deprivation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
sodium retention is a normal adaptive response to sodium deprivation.
the body can retain sodium when the diet is low in sodium and the intake of sodium increases, even if the intake of calories is low.
sodium intake should be limited for those with high blood pressure, even if they are obese.
